metadata.title: Claude Code, Opened.
metadata.subtitle: What's actually in Anthropic's public repo — the honest inventory
metadata.purpose: Walk the anthropics/claude-code GitHub repo with real cloc/git data and show that the 'source code' most people assume is there is not. The load-bearing artifact is a 5,248-line CHANGELOG and a set of community plugins. The compiled binary ships separately. That finding is the lesson.
metadata.source: anthropics/claude-code cloned 2026-08-01; all data computed via git log, find, wc -l. See REPO-VERIFY.md.
metadata.notes: Kokoro am_onyx, free (IN-FOR-BEAR LAW). GATE P before any ElevenLabs swap. Deep-explainer on ai-explainer chassis. 4 acts, 15 body beats. BEAT MIX: VOX 0% (WARN — no archival stills needed; GitHub skin IS the documentary texture for a code repo; flagged in BUILD-LOG.md) / MANIM 33% (B04, B05, B05b, B07, B10) / REMOTION 40% (B03, B08, B11, B11b, B13, B14) / CARD 27% (B02, B06, B09, B12). GATE VERIFY: all numbers in REPO-VERIFY.md. Never publish.

beats.narration_text: Annyeong — this is Liam, in for Bear. Anthropic's Claude Code has a public GitHub repo. Everyone assumes it's the source code. We're going to clone it, count the files, and see what's actually load-bearing. The answer is not what you think.

beats.narration_text: Up front: Claude Code ships as a compiled binary. The public GitHub repo is NOT the source. What you get is 210 files — half of them Markdown — a 5,248-line CHANGELOG documenting 353 releases, community plugins, deployment examples, and the scripts that manage the repo's own issue tracker. That's the public surface. The internals ship separately, compiled. This video opens every folder.

beats.narration_text: Here's the repo. Two hundred and ten files. Twenty-six megabytes on disk. The first thing a serious reader asks isn't 'how many stars' — it's 'where's the code.' Let's start there.

beats.narration_text: Extension breakdown — the actual inventory. One hundred and six Markdown files. That is half the repository. Twenty-one shell scripts. Twenty-one Python files. Eight Terraform configuration files. Five TypeScript files. Zero compiled JavaScript. Zero dist folders. This is not a source repo.

beats.narration_text: Folder inventory confirms it. CHANGELOG.md — 5,248 lines. README.md — 72 lines. Then examples, plugins, scripts, dot-claude commands. No src directory. No dist. No compiled output anywhere. If you came looking for the internals, the repo says plainly: they are not here.

beats.narration_text: The five TypeScript files are in scripts/ and they're not the tool — they're the issue tracker. Auto-close duplicates. Triage labels. Issue lifecycle. Sweep. This is GitHub maintenance code, not Claude Code internals. The source is not here. That's the finding.

beats.narration_text: The CHANGELOG is 5,248 lines and documents 353 releases — from version 0.2.21 to 2.1.220. At this cadence, Anthropic is shipping Claude Code roughly twice per day. That is the real clock in this repo. Not the commit count. Not the file count. The release velocity.

beats.narration_text: Here's a real entry. Version 2.1.219 — the most detailed release in the top ten. Opus Five added as default. A new network allowlist setting. A DirectoryAdded hook. Seven bug fixes across platform, keyboard, and session edges. This is the product's public interface. You are reading the surface of a compiled tool.

beats.narration_text: Strip the bot: 46 human commits in six months. Not a slow team — this is a public surface repo mirroring internal releases. The actual development is happening elsewhere, in a private codebase, and arriving here only as CHANGELOG entries when the bot fires.

beats.narration_text: Here's the verdict. The anthropics/claude-code GitHub repo is a public ledger, not a source repository. The compiled binary ships separately — you use it every day; you never see its internals here. What you DO get: 353 release entries that track every fix and feature since version 0.2.21; community plugins you can clone and adapt; gateway deployment examples in Terraform and shell; and the scripts that keep this repo's own issues organized. That's real value. It's just not the source code.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt. Point this at any public GitHub repo you assume is 'the source code' — a popular open source tool, a framework you depend on, anything. Run: git clone the repo, then find dot type f excluding dot git, pipe to sed to extract extensions, sort, uniq-count, sort descending. Ask Claude: what's load-bearing here — the code, the docs, or the config? Before you run it, write down your prediction. The gap between your prediction and the file inventory is exactly where the learning is. Take this prompt. Run it on a repo you use every day.
